Name: dormant_knowledge_override
Title: Knowing Yet Not Saying: A Heuristic Override That Suppresses Stored Facts
Short Hypothesis: In some failures, the model has correctly retrieved a fact internally (decodable at mid layers) but a competing surface heuristic-such as favoring a frequent or recently-mentioned token-overrides it in late layers, producing a wrong answer. Identifying and ablating the override component should recover the correct answer, demonstrating a genuine knowing-vs-saying gap.
Related Work: Work on the reversal curse and on hallucination treats failures as absence of knowledge. Studies of 'competing circuits' (e.g., copy vs recall heads) and of in-context vs parametric conflict (Yu et al., 2023) hint at arbitration. We specifically target cases where parametric knowledge is present yet suppressed by a non-contextual heuristic, and test recovery via targeted ablation-distinguishing suppression from ignorance.
Abstract: A model that answers a factual question incorrectly is usually assumed not to know the answer. We challenge this by isolating a class of failures in which the correct object is linearly decodable from internal states yet is overridden at output by a surface heuristic. Using an attribute probe, we filter QA failures into 'internally-correct' and 'internally-wrong' subsets. For the internally-correct subset, we search for the late-layer components-attention heads or MLP neurons-that inject the wrong, heuristic-preferred token, using logit attribution and activation patching. We hypothesize that a small set of 'override' components is responsible, that these components track heuristic features (token frequency, recency, string similarity to the subject) rather than the relation, and that ablating or down-weighting them converts a measurable fraction of failures into correct answers without harming previously-correct examples. We further characterize when the override wins as a function of the strength gap between the retrieved-fact direction and the heuristic direction in the final residual stream. This provides mechanistic evidence for a knowing-vs-saying dissociation and yields a concrete, ablation-based intervention that improves accuracy by unlocking already-stored knowledge, distinct from methods that add or edit facts.
Experiments: 1. Run factual QA; use an attribute probe to split failures into internally-correct vs internally-wrong. 2. On internally-correct failures, apply direct logit attribution to find components boosting the wrong token; corroborate with activation patching. 3. Characterize implicated components by correlating their outputs with heuristic features (frequency, recency, edit distance). 4. Ablate/down-scale override components; measure conversion of failures to correct and any collateral degradation on a correct-answer control set. 5. Model the win condition via the dot-product gap between fact and heuristic directions. Metrics: recovery rate, collateral error rate, component count, heuristic-feature correlation.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The probe may overstate internal correctness. Ablations can have diffuse side effects; a clean control is essential. The heuristic taxonomy may be incomplete. Recovery may be small in magnitude, limiting practical impact even if the mechanism is real.
